judgments.rationale: Integration by parts and the enclosed-area calculation dominate the item; the extrema coordinates also explicitly assess differentiation as an application.
The roots and their sum are complex-number work. The exact cosine evaluation is a separate scored trigonometric method, so it belongs as a secondary rather than a primary skill.
The graph sketch, restriction for invertibility, inverse domain, and inverse formula directly assess graph transformations and functions/inverses; the trigonometric form is supplied structure.
Both the singular-system condition and the subsequent solution are handled by elimination/row reduction; algebraic rearrangement is not an independent skill.
The dot product and obtuse-angle condition are vector geometry. Solving the resulting inequality is a distinct supporting algebra component, not a primary vector skill.
Implicit differentiation is explicitly required, and the perpendicular-tangent conclusion is a scored geometric application of the derivatives.
The solution uses the complex root, logarithmic identities, Vieta/root-sum and root-product relations, and polynomial coefficients; all three labels are mark-bearing.
Poisson calculations, grouped-data estimates and model-fit evidence, and the final conditional Poisson calculation are all explicitly scored.

The compound-angle identity is the central algebraic method. The final range is obtained from a graph of p as a function of q, which warrants a secondary graph skill but not a primary Functions topic.

The markscheme obtains f by integrating the supplied second derivative twice and then applying both boundary conditions; integration, rather than generic differentiation, is the materially assessed operation.
Both parameter recovery and the final probability use the stated normal model and standardization.
The first-principles limit is the definition of differentiation; the algebraic expansion and cancellation are supporting steps.
Factor and derivative-factor conditions are used to obtain polynomial coefficient relations; differentiation is only the theorem condition P'(5)=0.
The overlap area is computed from two triangles and two circular sectors using the cosine rule and sector-minus-triangle formulas; inverse-trigonometric notation is incidental.
The scored work sketches the two rational-function branches and determines asymptotes/parameters from the graph; inverse-function methods are not used.

The item materially assesses a function and its inverse together with graph interpretation/transformation. Differentiation is a supporting calculus component in the inflexion analysis, not a Functions skill.
The limit-comparison and convergence arguments are the only materially assessed methods.
The first part is a L’Hôpital limit and the second explicitly applies integration to the resulting limit expression; both methods earn marks.
The differential equation, Taylor coefficients and approximation error require the stated DE work, repeated differentiation, and Taylor/series reasoning.
Euler’s method, solving the differential equation, and the isocline/normal comparison are explicitly assessed differential-equation and derivative methods.

Euclidean gcd, divisibility of a Diophantine equation, and its integer solution family are number-theory work plus a distinct equation-solving component. Algebraic manipulation is routine support, not an additional tag.
Base-5 arithmetic and the divisibility equivalence are modular/number-theory work, while the if-and-only-if proof is explicitly mark-bearing.
The recurrence relation, its closed form, and the infection-week calculation are sequence/recurrence methods; the modelling limitations are contextual.
Eulerian-circuit reasoning, Kruskal, Dijkstra, and the route-inspection pairing are all graph algorithms. Counting and combinatorics is not the assessed method.

The question proves commutativity, associativity, and the Abelian-group axioms for a custom operation. The legacy group-operation label and proof method are supported; routine expansion is not a separate algebra tag.
De Morgan’s law is proved and a set intersection is enumerated. Set/relations content and proof are assessed, while algebraic manipulation is only incidental.
The eight-mark core proves an equivalence relation, and the class is identified as a line through a given point. Relation/set proof is primary; the geometric line description is a distinct secondary.
Composition, non-commutation, and the inverse of f are directly assessed function operations; the legacy paper option does not change the mathematical ownership.
The coset-style disjointness, bijection, and cardinality argument is group/set theory proved through explicit injectivity and surjectivity reasoning; algebraic manipulation is not independent.
The Poisson assumptions supply the variance and second moments; the entire item is a discrete-random-variable calculation.
Unbiased estimates, confidence intervals and the belief test use descriptive sample quantities, the normal model, and statistical inference.
The fish problem explicitly scores normal probabilities, a hypothesis test, correlation p-value, and regression, with descriptive summaries supporting the inference.

A geometric random variable and its probability generating function are the central content; the derivatives used to obtain E(X) are supporting calculus, and a broad probability-model tag adds no separate method.
The population law is a first-order differential equation solved by separation of variables; logarithmic algebra is enabling work rather than the mathematical topic.
The geometric-series expansion and the power series for arctan are the materially assessed methods.
Both parts are comparison/ratio tests for convergence of infinite series.
The entire nine-mark solution is a repeated L’Hôpital limit evaluation; differentiation is the tool, not an independently assessed skill.
The 11-mark solution solves the differential equation and the horizontal-tangent part is a property of its solution family.
Nearest-neighbour, deleted-vertex/MST reasoning and bipartite-graph analysis are graph-theory methods. Counting and combinatorics is not independently assessed.
The Euclidean algorithm and linear Diophantine solution family are number theory plus equation solving; the legacy number-theory label is intentional and algebraic manipulation alone is too weak.
Both first- and second-degree recurrence relations are solved as sequences; no independent proof or calculus method is required.
Fermat’s little theorem, congruence manipulation, and solving the quadratic congruence are directly modular-number-theory work; graph theory and induction are unsupported.
Identity, inverses, associativity and distributivity of binary operations are the legacy group/operation content, with complex arithmetic explicitly in the domain and formulas.
The non-Abelian group proof and Cayley-table completion are group-theory/set-structure work; proof is materially assessed, while routine algebra is not.
Closure, identity and inverses are proved for a multiplicative group. The legacy group label and proof method are supported; algebraic expansion is supporting work.
The real-domain map is proved bijective and the integer-domain map is shown non-surjective; this is directly functions/inverses content.
The PDF is normalized, integrated to form a CDF, and used for a median and interval probability; continuous-random-variable content dominates.
Each part uses sums of normally distributed service times and a normal probability. No descriptive-statistics summary or conditional-probability operation is independently assessed.
The sample estimates, confidence interval and one-sided test are normal-model statistical inference supported by descriptive sample calculations.
Perpendicularity is established by a vector dot product. Solving the resulting quadratic in k is a distinct secondary algebra step.
Polynomial remainder/factor and real-root reasoning carry the main work. The graph stretch and Poisson equation are independently scored secondary components.
Line intersection, parameters, vectors and quadrilateral area are primary vector geometry; the polygon-selection counts are a separate combinatorics component.
The sine-area relation and the two possible third sides are entirely triangle-geometry work.
The camera rate is a related-rates problem: the markscheme differentiates the geometric relation and evaluates the instantaneous rate.
Symmetry gives the upper tail and the second part explicitly conditions on X being above the lower threshold.
The scored work interprets areas under f′ to recover values of f and then sketches f; the precise method is an application of integration.
Integration is the dominant nine-mark calculation, while the two preceding identities are independently proved and belong as a trigonometric secondary.
The tangent is found from the derivative and then used to obtain the x-axis intercept, an explicit differentiation application.
Waveform amplitudes, phase shifts and the product graph are primary graph/transformation work. Average power is independently computed by integration.
The geometric-sequence structure and root-product/sum argument determine the remaining roots; logarithms only express the given roots.
Mean, standard deviation and the unchanged median are the only scored statistical methods.
The entire solution is integration by parts for an antiderivative involving ln x.
The PDF and expectation make continuous random variables primary. Integration by parts and the product-rule derivative are independently mark-bearing calculus methods.
Translation, range, intersections and graph features are primary function/graph work; the tangent-through-origin condition separately assesses differentiation and its application.
A two-unit horizontal translation is substituted and expanded; the assessed concept is graph transformation, not inverse functions.
The substitution u=sin x is used to rewrite and integrate the expression; trigonometry is only the supplied substitution.
